urgency.h: HR Protects the Company. We Protect You.
urgency.sub: You've been told to "keep it professional," to "not make it a thing," to "let HR handle it." Here's what actually happens next.

cards.p: The company's investigation exists to create a paper record that they "took it seriously." It rarely exists to fix anything. Meanwhile, the harasser is still there — and so are you.

Cut hours. A sudden bad review. A transfer. A layoff "for budget reasons" two months after you complained. Retaliation for reporting harassment is illegal on its own — and it usually makes the case bigger, not smaller.

cards.t: You do not have to quit to have a case
cards.p: Many people think they need to leave first. You don't. And if the environment became so intolerable you had no choice but to resign, the law treats that as being fired.

result_highlight: Under California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, harassment victims can recover lost wages, emotional-distress damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees — and both the company and the individual harasser can be held liable. The employer that ignored you is about to pay attention.

value.h: The Law Puts a Price on What They Did
value.sub: You're not asking for a favor. You're claiming what California law already says you're owed.

items.p: The anxiety before every shift. The sleepless nights. The therapy. Juries in harassment cases regularly award substantial damages for the human toll — because it's the core of the harm.
If you were pushed out, demoted, denied a promotion, or forced to quit — back pay, front pay, and lost benefits are all on the table.
When a company knew and did nothing, or protected the harasser because he was "valuable," the jury can award punitive damages designed to make sure it never happens again.
In California, the individual harasser can be personally liable — not just the company. That changes how seriously everyone takes it.
The employer pays your legal fees when you win under FEHA. Which is why the review is free and you never pay us unless we recover.

faq.q: What counts as sexual harassment at work?
faq.a: Two kinds. "Quid pro quo" — a boss or supervisor ties your job, raise, schedule, or promotion to sexual favors. And "hostile work environment" — unwanted comments, jokes, images, touching, or advances severe or frequent enough to make work miserable. It can come from a supervisor, a coworker, a customer, or a vendor. It does not have to be physical.

faq.q: I never reported it. Do I still have a case?
faq.a: Very possibly. Many people don't report because they're afraid — and the law understands that. Reporting can strengthen a case, but not reporting doesn't end it. Tell us what happened and we'll tell you honestly where you stand.

Your consultation is completely confidential. Most cases settle privately, and settlements typically include confidentiality. We will never contact your employer until you decide you want to move forward.
